title: Provider tokens live server-side; the browser holds an opaque handle only
context: The session-bridge chooses between two shapes that both work as sign-in ceremonies. The first: the browser holds an opaque server-issued handle, and provider tokens (access, id, refresh) live on a server-side record keyed by the handle. The second: the browser holds a JWT or a similar structured credential the provider issued, and the server re-verifies on every request. The rcf-lite tier this blueprint targets is small greenfield projects with one deployable and a session-record store that is either in-memory (for a scratch project) or a small table on a persistence blueprint (SQLite or D1). At that tier the opaque-handle shape reads simpler, hides the provider token graph from the browser, and makes sign-out a single delete against the server-side store.
decision: The session-bridge issues an opaque-handle cookie; provider tokens (access, id, refresh) are stored on the server-side session record keyed by the handle. The cookie value is neither the access token, the id_token, nor a refresh token; nothing exposed on `request.auth` is a provider token; nothing rendered into the client tier is a provider token. The reduced Principal (`principalId`, `provider`, `email?`, `roles[]`, `organisationIds[]`) is the only claim shape downstream code sees. `principalId` is derived from `{provider.id, subject}` so a user signed in through two providers is two principals unless the project's `enrichPrincipal` hook declares otherwise.
consequences: Sign-out is one delete; refresh-token reuse detection is one lookup; a compromised session record has server-side revocation as an option. The trade is a server-side store per session; that store is a project responsibility (in-memory in the reference wiring; a table on a composed persistence blueprint otherwise). A project whose deployable count grows beyond one and whose sessions must be shared across processes is naturally led to a persistence-backed session store; the composition path is clean because the session-bridge injects the store.

alternativesConsidered.name: JWT-in-cookie (browser holds a project-signed JWT)
alternativesConsidered.summary: The cookie value is a signed JWT the browser round-trips on every request; the session-bridge verifies signature and reads the claims.
alternativesConsidered.reasonNotChosen: Common at scale where a stateless server is a hard constraint; carries no server-side revocation without a companion revocation-list mechanism, and puts identity claims on a token the browser holds (a footprint an XSS can lift). The rcf-lite tier does not need the statelessness enough to pay those costs.

alternativesConsidered.name: Provider access token as the cookie
alternativesConsidered.summary: The browser holds the provider's access token directly.
alternativesConsidered.reasonNotChosen: Leaks the vendor's token surface into every browser side-channel, ties revocation to the vendor's clock, and rules out multi-provider composition (a single cookie shape cannot represent N provider tokens at once).
